newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa's Boesak charged over missing aid money.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa's Boesak charged over missing aid money.

text.p: Allan Boesak, the black cleric who battled apartheid with Archbishop Desmond Tutu through five bleak years of South African emergency rule, was charged in absentia on Friday with fraud and theft from Western donors.
State prosecutor Steven Powell told Reuters that Boesak, who is teaching theology in California, and former bookkeeper Freddie Steenkamp faced nine counts of fraud and 21 counts of theft.

He said the victims included Scandinavian aid agencies, Coca Cola and American musician Paul Simon, who donated proceeds from his Gracelands album, recorded partly in South Africa, to anti-apartheid projects managed by Boesak.
"We are arranging the (court) appearance of Dr Boesak. His lawyers have told us he will be coming back on his own accord," Powell said.

Boesak, who headed the anti-apartheid Foundation for Peace and Justice, has been under investigation for more than two years over the alleged disappearance or misuse of mainly Danish and Swedish aid funds totalling close to two million rand ($422,000).
Boesak has denied any wrongdoing and was cleared in an investigation by lawyers appointed by South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki.
But donors including DanChurch Aid insisted on a further investigation and the case was handed to the South African Office for Serious Economic Offences.
"The fraud charge relates to different projects the foundation had...The amount involved is just over a million rand in respect of each of them (Boesak and Steenkamp).
"The funds were donated to the foundation and they used them for themselves," Powell said.
The charges were put to Steenkamp in the Cape Town magistrates' court on Friday. He was released on bail of 2,000 rand, had to surrender his passport and was ordered to report to police each Sunday.
The case was adjourned to January 17 next year.

Christian Balslev-Olesen, secretary-general of DanChurch Aid, one of the groups which originally levelled accusations of financial abuse at Boesak, said his organisation was pleased progress was being made in the investigation.
"It is a great relief for us that there will soon be a ruling in this case after two and a half years of extensive investigation and uncertainty," he told Reuters in Copenhagen.
"Beyond that I have nothing to say at this stage."
Boesak and Tutu led the black struggle against apartheid during five years of emergency rule, which saw thousands of black opposition activists jailed without charge in the 1980s.
Boesak's reputation was dented, however, by two highly publicised affairs. After the second scandal, Boesak divorced his wife Dorothy and married television personality Elna Botha.
Boesak, 50, said in an interview with South Africa's You magazine last week that he would return to South Africa to face the charges even at risk of going to jail.
"I might be called back to South Africa any day. And I will go if they want to prosecute me. I have no choice. I will not run away," he told the magazine.
Saying he had a renewed vocation, Boesak, once president of the Geneva-based World Alliance of Reformed Churches representing over 70 million Calvinists, said he hoped to return to the ministry.
He said he had been supported since his dismissal from his church and other posts by friends including former Atlanta mayor Andrew Young.
